rv.q: Meera Syal’s heartbreaking, and surely award-winning, performance will make you weep.
Pooja Ghai’s production rallies when it gets acrimonious, and only improves from there, with the ensemble really hitting their stride.
The production has a nice dreamlike quality, with Queenie's visions of her past life adding to an affecting family drama.
It’s all a bit of a muddle: a play of many parts, struggling to find their sum.
This is, unfortunately, not a piece of new writing worthy of the National Theatre.
An utterly compelling watch, I was thoroughly engaged from start to finish.
Gupta allows for the possibility that Ameet has come to guide Queenie through this last chapter and accompany her to the next life.
A Tupperware of Ashes has crafted a formidable character, and one that will be remembered.

The subject matter is resolutely affecting, with the impact of Queenie’s deterioration both upsetting to witness and on occasions even frightening - a testament to Syal’s total embodiment of the character.
This is an arresting piece of work that would be deserving of a larger audience in the Lyttleton.
Nitin Sawhney’s superb music likewise deepens the drama’s emotional journey.
A Ashes is exceptional on every front.

cn.t: Gupta's dementia drama earns praise for Meera Syal's towering performance and moments of humor amid tragedy, though some critics find it overly linear and struggling to coalesce. Most appreciate its nuanced portrayal of a British-Indian family navigating loss.
